lesson.title: The Sweet Spot of Pressure: Why Too Little or Too Much Arousal Hurts Performance
lesson.summary: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes an inverted U shaped relationship between arousal and performance, with performance weakest at very low and very high arousal and strongest at a moderate level that shifts depending on how difficult the task is.
lesson.body:
Arousal theory already establishes that organisms are motivated to maintain a preferred level of physiological and mental activation, not simply to reduce arousal to zero the way a strict drive-reduction account might suggest. If some intermediate level of arousal is generally preferred, it is a natural next step to ask exactly how arousal relates to how well a person actually performs a task. That is the specific question the Yerkes-Dodson law answers.

The law traces back to early twentieth century research, commonly associated with psychologists Robert Yerkes and John Dodson, who studied how varying levels of stimulation affected learning and performance on a discrimination task. The general finding, replicated conceptually many times since in different forms, is that performance is poor when arousal is very low, improves as arousal rises to a moderate level, and then declines again if arousal keeps climbing into a range that feels overwhelming or stressful. Plotted on a graph, performance against arousal traces an inverted U shape rather than a straight line.

The law has a second, often overlooked part: the position of that optimal point is not fixed, it depends on the difficulty of the task. For difficult, unfamiliar, or complex tasks, the optimal level of arousal tends to be lower, because high arousal narrows attention and adds interference that a demanding task cannot easily absorb. For simple, familiar, or well practiced tasks, a higher level of arousal can be tolerated, or even helpful, since there is less complexity for the extra activation to disrupt.

Everyday experience matches this pattern reasonably well. A student who feels absolutely no nervousness before an exam may lack the motivation to prepare seriously, while a student who feels overwhelming panic may blank on material they actually know, and the sweet spot for most people sits somewhere between those extremes, often experienced as focused, purposeful nervousness. An experienced musician, having rehearsed a piece until it is nearly automatic, may perform it well even under the high arousal of a stressful audition, while attempting to sight read a completely new and difficult piece under that same pressure would likely go far worse, exactly the difficulty dependent shift the Yerkes-Dodson law describes.
